To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
We have identified genes, pathways and biological processes that are differentially regulated in human chondrocyte cells between healthy and osteoarthritic cartilage.

we have performed a comprehensive integrative study of OA progression in primary human chondrocyte samples, identifying key players that replicate across independent data sets and have translational potential.
we have integrated epigenomics, RNA-sequencing and quantitative proteomics to investigate genes and pathways implicated in osteoartritis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of novel genes and pathways involved at the molecular level in OA progression.
the molecular changes that occur in chondrocyte cells as a result of the development and progression of osteoarthritis (a joint degenerative disease).

the identification of novel biomarkers and pathways involved in the pathogenesis of osteoarthritis (Osteoarthritis) and the translation of this knowledge into new diagnostic tools, prognostic biomarkers and therapeutic targets.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this study provides a first integrated epigenomic, transcriptomic and proteomic view of human primary chondoctytes, and identifies key molecular markers in osteoarhritis progression.
our study provides a resource for the OA research community and has identified key genes and pathways involved OA progression.

we have identified 49 genes that are differentially regulated at multiple omics level in human primary chondroyctes between intact and degraded artifical cartilage, 16 of them have not previously been linked with OA and we have replicated these results using independent datasets.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the molecular landscape of chondrocyte OA can be characterized by the following genes/proteins: AQP1 (aquaporin-1), COL1A1 (collagen alpha 1 (I) chain), CLEC3B (C-type lectin domain containing 3B), MMP1 (collagenase 1), MMP13 (collagenase-3), and TIMP1 (tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinase-1).
we have identified 16 new candidate genes for OA and that we have identified a set of genes, pathways and processes that are likely to be important in the pathophysiology of OA.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the integration of multiple omics data from the same sample can be used to generate a more comprehensive view of the molecular changes that underpin complex diseases.
a combination of multiple omics technologies can be used in a single experiment to provide a comprehensive view of the underlying biology of a disease.
OA is a complex, multi-factorial disease and the molecular pathways involved in OA progression are not limited to a single tissue type or cellular process.
